solution:
The deciding factor is whether the molecule can hydrogen bond with water.

Glucose \(\text{(C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6)\) carries five \(-\text{OH}\) groups (the formation of glucose pentaacetate on acetylation shows there are five of them) besides its carbonyl group, and sucrose carries eight. Every one of these \(-\text{OH}\) groups is strongly polar and can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, so a large number of hydrogen bonds form between the sugar and the surrounding water molecules. The energy released on forming these bonds more than compensates for breaking the hydrogen bonds already present in water, so the sugars dissolve freely.

Cyclohexane \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12})\) and benzene \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_6)\) are pure hydrocarbons. They have no \(-\text{OH}\) or other polar group, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water at all; their molecules are held only by weak van der Waals forces. Dissolving them would mean breaking the hydrogen-bonded structure of water without anything to replace it, which is energetically unfavourable.

Hence glucose and sucrose are water soluble while cyclohexane and benzene are not, even though all four are six-membered ring compounds — ring size is irrelevant, the polar hydroxyl groups are what matter.

Lactose is a disaccharide built from one \(\beta\)-D-galactose unit and one \(\beta\)-D-glucose unit, joined by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of galactose and C4 of glucose.

Hydrolysis breaks that glycosidic linkage, the oxide bridge being cleaved by the addition of one molecule of water. Each monosaccharide unit is therefore set free.

Products: one molecule of D-galactose and one molecule of D-glucose (an equimolar mixture).

In the solid state and in solution, D-glucose exists very largely not as the open-chain aldehyde but as a cyclic hemiacetal: the \(-\text{OH}\) group on C-5 adds across the \(-\text{CHO}\) group to give a six-membered (pyranose) ring. The carbon that was the aldehyde carbon becomes C-1 of the ring and carries a new hydroxyl group, the anomeric \(-\text{OH}\). The two cyclic forms and the open chain form are in equilibrium, so a free \(-\text{CHO}\) group can still be generated as the ring opens.

Acetylation with acetic anhydride esterifies all five hydroxyl groups, and this includes the anomeric \(-\text{OH}\) at C-1. Once C-1 carries an acetate group instead of a hydroxyl, the ring is locked shut — it can no longer open to the open-chain aldehyde form.

Since no free \(-\text{CHO}\) group can be produced, glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine to give an oxime, which is exactly what is observed. The aldehyde group is not destroyed; it is simply no longer available, because the ring cannot reopen.

An amino acid carries an acidic \(-\text{COOH}\) group and a basic \(-\text{NH}_2\) group in the same molecule. In the solid state and in aqueous solution the carboxyl group loses a proton to the amino group of the same molecule, giving a dipolar ion or zwitter ion, \(\text{R}-\text{CH}(\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3)-\text{COO}^-\). The molecule is overall neutral but carries a full positive and a full negative charge.

Melting point: the crystal is therefore held together by strong electrostatic (ion–ion) attractions, exactly as in a salt, rather than by the weaker dipole–dipole and hydrogen-bonding forces that hold a halo acid crystal together. A great deal more thermal energy is needed to pull the lattice apart, so amino acids are high-melting solids.

Solubility: the same charges give strong ion–dipole interaction with water, so amino acids dissolve readily in water.

A halo acid such as chloroacetic acid, \(\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}\), has no basic group, so it cannot form an internal salt; it stays as neutral molecules and consequently melts lower and is less soluble in water.

Hence the higher melting points and higher water solubility of amino acids are both traced to their zwitter ionic, salt-like character.

Egg white is an aqueous solution of the globular protein albumin. On boiling, the protein is denatured: the hydrogen bonds holding the native structure are disturbed, the globules unfold and the uncoiled polypeptide chains become entangled with one another, so the protein coagulates into an insoluble semi-solid mass. This is the familiar setting of egg white.

The water is not chemically consumed and it does not all evaporate. It is held within the network of the coagulated protein — trapped and adsorbed in the meshes of the entangled, unfolded chains — so the boiled egg feels dry even though the water is still present in it. A small part escapes as steam.

Answer: the water is retained, absorbed and trapped inside the coagulated (denatured) protein mass.

Vitamins are classified by solubility. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) belongs to the water soluble group, along with the B group vitamins.

Because it is soluble in water, vitamin C is freely filtered by the kidneys and is readily excreted in the urine; it is not taken up and held in the liver or in adipose (fat storing) tissue the way the fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are. So the body has no store of it.

Answer: vitamin C cannot be stored because it is a water soluble vitamin and is readily excreted in urine — which is why it must be supplied regularly in the diet.

A nucleotide is made of three parts: a nitrogenous base joined to the 1' position of a pentose sugar (that much is the nucleoside), with phosphoric acid esterified at the 5' position of the sugar. In DNA the pentose sugar is \(\beta\)-D-2-deoxyribose.

Complete hydrolysis cleaves both linkages — the base–sugar bond and the sugar–phosphate ester bond — so all three components are released.

Products: thymine (the base), \(\beta\)-D-2-deoxyribose (the sugar) and phosphoric acid, \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\).

In a double stranded nucleic acid the two chains are held together by hydrogen bonds between specific pairs of bases — adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine always pairs with guanine. Because every base on one strand is matched by its partner on the other, such a molecule must contain adenine and thymine in equal amounts, and cytosine and guanine in equal amounts. A fixed quantitative relationship among the bases is thus a direct consequence of two complementary strands.

RNA shows no such relationship among the quantities of its bases. Therefore its bases cannot be paired off one-for-one against a partner chain.

Conclusion: RNA is not a double stranded molecule. It is single stranded — a single helical chain, which may fold back on itself, but which has no complementary second strand imposing equal base amounts.

A monosaccharide is a carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed further to give a simpler unit of polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone. It is therefore the simplest carbohydrate unit.

About 20 monosaccharides occur in nature. They are further classified by the number of carbon atoms and by the functional group present: one containing an aldehyde group is an aldose, one containing a keto group is a ketose — hence aldohexose, ketohexose, aldopentose and so on.

Examples: glucose (an aldohexose), fructose (a ketohexose) and ribose (an aldopentose).

Reducing sugars are those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent.

A carbohydrate does this when it has a free aldehydic or ketonic group — that is, a free anomeric carbon able to open to the carbonyl form.

All monosaccharides, whether aldose or ketose, are reducing sugars. Among the disaccharides, those in which the reducing group of one unit is left free are also reducing sugars, for example maltose and lactose. Sucrose is not a reducing sugar, because the reducing groups of both its glucose and fructose units are used up in forming the glycosidic linkage.

(i) Storage of energy. Carbohydrates act as the food storage material of the plant — starch is the main storage polysaccharide of plants and is the reserve from which the plant draws glucose.

(ii) Structural support. Cellulose is the predominant constituent of the cell wall of plant cells, and it is this that gives the plant its rigidity and mechanical strength.

The test is behaviour on hydrolysis: a monosaccharide cannot be hydrolysed to anything simpler, whereas a disaccharide yields two monosaccharide units.

Monosaccharides: ribose (an aldopentose), 2-deoxyribose (an aldopentose), galactose (an aldohexose) and fructose (a ketohexose).

Disaccharides: maltose (which gives two molecules of D-glucose) and lactose (which gives one molecule each of D-galactose and D-glucose).

When two monosaccharide units join to form a disaccharide or a polysaccharide, they are held together by an oxide linkage formed by the loss of a molecule of water between two of their hydroxyl groups. This linkage between two monosaccharide units through an oxygen atom is called a glycosidic linkage.

For example, in sucrose the glycosidic linkage runs between C1 of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and C2 of \(\beta\)-D-fructose; in maltose it runs between C1 of one \(\alpha\)-D-glucose unit and C4 of the other.

Glycogen is the polysaccharide in which carbohydrate is stored in the animal body. It is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and is also called animal starch because its structure resembles that of amylopectin. It is present in the liver, muscles and brain, and also occurs in yeast and fungi; when the body needs glucose, enzymes break glycogen down to glucose.

Differences from starch:

(i) Source — starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, glycogen that of animals.

(ii) Composition — starch is a mixture of two components, the water-soluble unbranched amylose (about 15–20%) and the water-insoluble branched amylopectin (about 80–85%). Glycogen is a single component with no amylose-like unbranched counterpart.

(iii) Extent of branching — glycogen has the same kind of structure as amylopectin (chains built by C1–C4 linkages with branching at C1–C6) but is rather more highly branched than amylopectin.

(i) Sucrose. The glycosidic linkage between C1 of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and C2 of \(\beta\)-D-fructose is cleaved, giving an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(–)-fructose:

\(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\)

Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory, but because the laevorotation of fructose \((-92.4^\circ)\) exceeds the dextrorotation of glucose \((+52.5^\circ)\) the product mixture is laevorotatory; it is therefore called invert sugar.

(ii) Lactose. The linkage between C1 of galactose and C4 of glucose is cleaved, giving one molecule of D-galactose and one molecule of D-glucose.

Both are polysaccharides of glucose, so the difference lies in which anomer is used and hence in how the chains are linked.

Starch is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose. Its unbranched component amylose has 200–1000 \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucose units joined by C1–C4 glycosidic linkages; its branched component amylopectin has chains formed by C1–C4 linkages with branching occurring through C1–C6 linkages.

Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide composed only of \(\beta\)-D-glucose units, joined by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of one glucose unit and C4 of the next. It is unbranched.

Basic structural difference: starch is built from \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and is branched (in amylopectin), whereas cellulose is built from \(\beta\)-D-glucose and is a straight, unbranched chain.

(i) With HI. On prolonged heating with \(\text{HI}\), D-glucose is completely reduced and gives n-hexane. All the oxygen-containing groups are removed, and the fact that a straight-chain alkane is obtained shows that the six carbon atoms of glucose are linked in a straight chain.

(ii) With bromine water. Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent and oxidises D-glucose to the six-carbon monocarboxylic acid, gluconic acid. Only the \(-\text{CHO}\) group is attacked, which shows that the carbonyl group of glucose is present as an aldehydic group.

(iii) With \(\text{HNO}_3\). Nitric acid is a stronger oxidising agent and oxidises both the terminal groups — the \(-\text{CHO}\) group and the primary alcoholic \(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) group — giving the dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid. Gluconic acid is likewise oxidised by \(\text{HNO}_3\) to saccharic acid. This shows the presence of a primary alcoholic group in glucose.

Three observations cannot be accounted for by the open chain (Fischer) structure of D-glucose:

(i) Although the open chain structure contains an aldehyde group, glucose does not give Schiff's test and does not form the hydrogensulphite addition product with \(\text{NaHSO}_3\) — reactions that a free \(-\text{CHO}\) group would be expected to give.

(ii) The pentaacetate of glucose does not react with hydroxylamine to form an oxime, indicating the absence of a free \(-\text{CHO}\) group in the pentaacetate.

(iii) Glucose exists in two different crystalline forms, called \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The \(\alpha\)-form, m.p. \(419\,\text{K}\), separates on crystallisation from a concentrated solution at \(303\,\text{K}\), while the \(\beta\)-form, m.p. \(423\,\text{K}\), separates from a hot saturated aqueous solution at \(371\,\text{K}\). An open chain structure offers no reason for two such forms.

All three are explained by the cyclic hemiacetal structure, in which the \(-\text{OH}\) at C-5 adds to the \(-\text{CHO}\) group to give a six-membered pyranose ring. The aldehyde group is no longer free, and the new hydroxyl at the anomeric carbon C-1 can point either way, which gives the two anomers \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose.

Amino acids which can be synthesised in the body are called non-essential amino acids. Those which cannot be synthesised in the body and must therefore be obtained through the diet are called essential amino acids; ten of the twenty natural amino acids fall in this class.

Examples of essential amino acids: valine and leucine (also isoleucine, arginine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and histidine).

Examples of non-essential amino acids: glycine and alanine (also glutamic acid, aspartic acid, glutamine, asparagine, serine, cysteine, tyrosine and proline).

(i) Peptide linkage. The amide linkage \(-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\) formed between the \(-\text{COOH}\) group of one amino acid and the \(-\text{NH}_2\) group of another, with the elimination of a molecule of water. It is the bond that joins amino acid residues in a protein. For example, glycine and alanine combine in this way to give the dipeptide glycylalanine.

(ii) Primary structure. Each polypeptide chain in a protein has its amino acids linked in one specific sequence; this sequence of amino acids is the primary structure of the protein. Any change in the sequence produces a different protein.

(iii) Denaturation. When a protein in its native form is subjected to a physical change such as a change in temperature, or a chemical change such as a change in pH, the hydrogen bonds are disturbed, the globules unfold, the helix uncoils and the protein loses its biological activity. This is denaturation. The secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed while the primary structure remains intact. Coagulation of egg white on boiling, and curdling of milk, are common examples.

The secondary structure of a protein is the shape in which the long polypeptide chain exists, and it arises from regular folding of the backbone through hydrogen bonding between the \(>\text{C}=\text{O}\) and \(-\text{NH}-\) groups of the peptide bonds.

Two types are found:

(i) \(\alpha\)-helix — the chain twists into a right handed screw, forming all possible hydrogen bonds.

(ii) \(\beta\)-pleated sheet — the chains are stretched out to nearly maximum extension and laid side by side, held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds, the arrangement resembling the pleated folds of drapery.

Hydrogen bonding stabilises the \(\alpha\)-helix.

The polypeptide chain twists into a right handed screw in such a way that it forms all possible hydrogen bonds: the \(-\text{NH}\) group of each amino acid residue is hydrogen bonded to the \(>\text{C}=\text{O}\) group of a residue in the adjacent turn of the helix.

These hydrogen bonds are intramolecular — they run within one and the same chain, between groups of the peptide bonds — and it is they that hold the coil in shape.

Fibrous proteins

(i) The polypeptide chains run parallel to one another and are held together by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bonds, giving a fibre-like, thread-like structure.

(ii) They are generally insoluble in water.

(iii) Examples: keratin, present in hair, wool and silk; myosin, present in muscles.

Globular proteins

(i) The polypeptide chains coil around to give a spherical, ball-like shape.

(ii) They are usually soluble in water.

(iii) Examples: insulin and albumins.

The essential difference is thus one of molecular shape — fibre-like with parallel chains, against spherical with coiled chains — and this in turn decides their solubility in water.

An amino acid contains an acidic \(-\text{COOH}\) group and a basic \(-\text{NH}_2\) group in the same molecule. In aqueous solution the carboxyl group loses a proton and the amino group accepts it, so the amino acid exists as a dipolar or zwitter ion:

\(\text{R}-\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)-\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{R}-\text{CH}(\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3)-\text{COO}^-\)

The zwitter ion is neutral overall but carries both a positive and a negative centre, and each centre can respond to the opposite kind of reagent:

With an acid, the \(-\text{COO}^-\) end accepts a proton, so the amino acid behaves as a base and gives the cation \(\text{R}-\text{CH}(\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3)-\text{COOH}\).

With a base, the \(-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\) end loses a proton, so the amino acid behaves as an acid and gives the anion \(\text{R}-\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)-\text{COO}^-\).

Because it can react both with acids and with bases, an amino acid is amphoteric.

[Textbook note on the figures quoted below: the chapter states the activation energy for the acid hydrolysis of sucrose as \(6.22\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and for hydrolysis by sucrase as \(2.15\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Both are roughly an order of magnitude below the accepted experimental values — the acid-catalysed inversion of sucrose runs at about \(107\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and the enzyme-catalysed route at about \(36\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). They are reproduced here because they are what the book teaches and what an examiner using it will expect, and the point they illustrate is unaffected: the enzyme lowers the activation-energy barrier by roughly a factor of three, and the book's own ratio \(6.22/2.15 = 2.9\) preserves that comparison even though the absolute magnitudes do not stand.] Enzymes are biocatalysts — substances that catalyse the chemical reactions occurring in living organisms and allow them to proceed under the very mild conditions found in the body.

Their chief characteristics:

(i) Almost all enzymes are globular proteins.

(ii) They are highly specific, each being active for a particular reaction and for a particular substrate.

(iii) They are needed only in very small quantities.

(iv) Like chemical catalysts they work by reducing the magnitude of the activation energy. For instance, the activation energy for the acid hydrolysis of sucrose is \(6.22\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), while it is only \(2.15\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) when sucrose is hydrolysed by the enzyme sucrase.

Enzymes are usually named after the substrate or the class of compounds on which they act, or after the reaction they catalyse, the name ending in -ase. For example maltase catalyses the hydrolysis of maltose to glucose, and the enzymes catalysing oxidation of one substrate with simultaneous reduction of another are called oxidoreductases.

On denaturation the hydrogen bonds holding the native protein are disturbed, the globules unfold and the helix uncoils.

Effect on structure: the secondary and tertiary structures of the protein are destroyed, while the primary structure — the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide linkages — remains intact, because the peptide bonds themselves are not broken.

Consequence: having lost its unique three-dimensional shape, the protein loses its biological activity. The denatured protein is also generally less soluble and coagulates, as when egg white sets on boiling or milk curdles.

Vitamins are classified on the basis of their solubility in water or in fat, into two groups:

(i) Fat soluble vitamins — soluble in fats and oils but insoluble in water. These are vitamins A, D, E and K. They are stored in the liver and in adipose (fat storing) tissue.

(ii) Water soluble vitamins — the B group vitamins and vitamin C. These must be supplied regularly in the diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored in the body, vitamin \(\text{B}_{12}\) being the exception.

Vitamin responsible for the coagulation of blood: vitamin K. Its deficiency causes an increased blood clotting time.

Vitamins are organic compounds required in the diet in small amounts to perform specific biological functions for the normal maintenance of optimum growth and health of the organism. They cannot be synthesised in our body, so they must be taken in the food; if they are not, a specific deficiency disease follows. This is why vitamin A and vitamin C are essential to us:

Vitamin A is needed for the health of the eye. Its deficiency causes xerophthalmia, a hardening of the cornea of the eye, and night blindness.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is needed for healthy gums and connective tissue. Its deficiency causes scurvy, marked by bleeding gums.

Important sources:

Vitamin A — fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk.

Vitamin C — citrus fruits, amla and green leafy vegetables.

Nucleic acids are the biomolecules present, along with proteins, in the chromosomes in the nucleus of a living cell, and they are responsible for the transmission of inherent characters from one generation to the next. Chemically they are long chain polymers of nucleotides, and so are also called polynucleotides; each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. They are of two kinds, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA).

Two important functions:

(i) Heredity. DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and the reserve of genetic information. It is capable of self-duplication during cell division, so that identical DNA strands are passed on to the daughter cells, and it maintains the identity of different species over millions of years.

(ii) Protein synthesis. Nucleic acids carry out the synthesis of proteins in the cell — the message for the synthesis of a particular protein is held in the DNA, while the proteins are actually synthesised by the RNA molecules.

A nucleoside is the unit formed when a nitrogenous base is attached to the 1' position of the pentose sugar. It therefore has two components:

nucleoside = base + pentose sugar

A nucleotide is formed when a nucleoside is further linked to phosphoric acid at the 5' position of its sugar. It therefore has three components:

nucleotide = base + pentose sugar + phosphate

The difference is thus the phosphate group: a nucleotide is a nucleoside carrying a phosphoric acid residue esterified at C-5' of the sugar. Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides, joined by phosphodiester linkages between the 5' and 3' carbon atoms of the pentose sugar.

In the double helix the two nucleic acid chains are wound about each other and held together by hydrogen bonds formed between specific pairs of bases: adenine forms hydrogen bonds only with thymine, and cytosine only with guanine.

This pairing is what fixes the relation between the strands. Wherever one strand carries adenine, the other must carry thymine opposite it; wherever one carries cytosine, the other must carry guanine. So the sequence of the second strand is completely determined by that of the first, but it is not a copy of it — at each position it carries the partner base, not the same base.

Hence the two strands are not identical; they are complementary. It is this complementarity that allows DNA to duplicate itself, since each strand can direct the building of a new partner strand.

Structural differences

(i) Sugar — DNA contains the pentose sugar \(\beta\)-D-2-deoxyribose, whereas RNA contains \(\beta\)-D-ribose.

(ii) Bases — both contain adenine, guanine and cytosine, but the fourth base is thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA.

(iii) Strands — DNA is a double stranded molecule, two complementary chains wound about each other as a double helix; RNA is a single stranded molecule, a single helix which sometimes folds back on itself.

Functional differences

(i) DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and the reserve of genetic information. It duplicates itself during cell division so that identical strands pass to the daughter cells, and it holds the coded message for the proteins to be synthesised.

(ii) RNA actually carries out the synthesis of proteins in the cell. It occurs in three types — messenger RNA (m-RNA), ribosomal RNA (r-RNA) and transfer RNA (t-RNA) — which perform different parts of this task.

Three types of RNA are found in the cell, and they perform different functions:

(i) messenger RNA (m-RNA)

(ii) ribosomal RNA (r-RNA)

(iii) transfer RNA (t-RNA)

Together these are the molecules that actually carry out the synthesis of proteins in the cell.
